title: Trump's Pharma Tariff Countdown Begins, Indian Generic Drugmakers Face Uncertain Future
excerpt: With a two-year grace period now ticking and 100% tariffs on generic drugs set for 2028, India's $8.7 billion pharmaceutical export pipeline to the US faces its biggest test yet.
body:
• Trump announced phased tariffs on imported generic drugs: 0% for two years starting August 1, 2026, rising to 100% in 2028 and 200% in 2029
  • India, the largest foreign supplier of generic medicines to the US, could be disproportionately affected, with companies like Sun Pharma, Dr Reddy's, and Cipla deriving 30-45% of revenues from the US market
  • Branded drug tariffs of up to 100% are already in effect, with a July 31 deadline for onshoring agreements that would reduce the rate to 20%
  • Industry analysts warn that razor-thin generic drug margins could lead to product discontinuations and drug shortages rather than US manufacturing reshoring

The Two-Year Clock Is Ticking

The pharmaceutical industry's long-anticipated reckoning with US trade policy entered a new phase this week as the two-year grace period for generic drug imports officially began. President Trump announced on July 21 that imported generic drugs would face a 0% tariff through August 2028, after which the rate would jump to 100% for one year and then 200% thereafter, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The announcement marks the first time the administration has set a specific timeline for tariffs on generic medicines, a category that had been exempted under the Section 232 pharmaceutical trade framework even as branded drugs faced levies of up to 100%. "This is done in order to RESHORE Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America, with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time given to them," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"The proposal introduces a significant long-term structural risk to export margins."

— Mayank Jain, Market Analyst at Share.Market by PhonePe

A $500 Billion Scramble

The generic drug tariff timeline arrives as the branded pharmaceutical industry is already deep into a massive reshoring push. According to Pharmaceutical Executive, the industry has collectively committed over $500 billion in US investment since the Section 232 tariffs were announced. Pfizer struck a $70 billion deal with the Trump administration in September 2025, securing a three-year tariff exemption. AstraZeneca pledged $50 billion in US manufacturing by 2030, while Johnson & Johnson committed $55 billion over four years, according to Reuters.

A July 31, 2026 deadline for branded drug companies to negotiate onshoring agreements — which would reduce tariffs from 100% to 20% — has added urgency. Ryan Last, a senior associate at Troutman Pepper Locke, told Pharmaceutical Executive that "the time for conceptual discussions has passed" and companies need "concrete, data-backed proposals." Companies that secured deals through the administration's most-favoured-nation pricing initiative, including commitments to sell drugs through the new TrumpRx.gov platform, received exemptions.

India's Generic Drug Empire at Stake

For India — which calls itself the "pharmacy of the world" — the generic drug tariff announcement carries particular weight. Indian drugmakers supply nearly half of all generic prescriptions filled in the US, and exports to America were worth $8.7 billion in fiscal 2024, roughly 31% of total pharma exports, according to the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India.

The impact is already being priced into markets. Shares of major Indian pharma companies fell sharply after Trump's announcement, with companies like Zydus Lifesciences and Dr Reddy's Laboratories — which derive approximately 45% and 43% of revenues from US sales respectively — considered most exposed, according to a Jefferies analysis. Sun Pharma, India's largest drugmaker, has about 30% of revenues from the US, though over half of its US sales come from patented drugs manufactured by contract organisations outside India, reducing its direct exposure.

The Indian Pharmaceutical Alliance, representing major drugmakers including Sun Pharma, Dr Reddy's, Cipla, and Zydus Lifesciences, has said it is "confident that continued dialogue among stakeholders will help address the subject," according to Reuters. Sun Pharma Managing Director Dilip Shanghvi has said any tariffs imposed would be passed on to consumers.

The Reshoring Paradox

Health policy experts have flagged a fundamental tension in the tariff plan. Generic drugs account for approximately 90% of prescriptions dispensed in the US but represent only a fraction of overall drug spending, according to The American Journal of Managed Care. Roughly 80% of active pharmaceutical ingredients used in the US are sourced from China and India. Building and validating new US manufacturing capacity typically takes five to ten years — well beyond the two-year runway Trump has offered.

The Association for Accessible Medicines, which represents generic drug manufacturers, warned that Medicaid inflation rebates and the 340B program already limit manufacturers' ability to raise prices, meaning added tariff costs could push manufacturers to exit low-margin markets altogether rather than invest in domestic production. Older injectable generics, including certain cancer drugs, are especially exposed given their already slim margins, the AJMC reported.

Indian drugmaker Cipla has begun hedging its bets, expanding its US manufacturing footprint with investments in complex respiratory product capacity at facilities in Fall River, Massachusetts, and Central Islip, New York, according to Reuters.

What's Next

The two-year window before generic tariffs take effect sets up 2028 as a pivotal year for drug affordability and supply chain stability. For the Indian diaspora in the US, the stakes are both professional and personal: thousands work in the pharmaceutical sector, and any disruption to generic drug supplies could affect the affordability of medications that millions of Americans — including Indian-Americans — rely on daily. With India's trade relationship with Washington now central to how this policy plays out, the countdown has begun.
nri_angle: Indian pharmaceutical companies that employ thousands of diaspora professionals face major revenue risk, while generic drug tariffs could raise medication costs for Indian-Americans who rely on affordable generics.
